newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinian prisoners protest in Israeli jails.
newsitem.headline: Palestinian prisoners protest in Israeli jails.

text.p: A PLO official accused Israel on Monday of denying Palestinian prisoners proper medical treatment and family visits, warning of an "explosion" in jails if conditions did not improve.

"Around 4,000 Palestinian prisoners in Israel's jails carried out a one-day hunger strike on Sunday as a warning to Israel that it could be resumed if their conditions were not improved," Hisham Abdel-Razek told Reuters.

"An explosion inside Israeli jails will take place if Israel continues to maltreat Palestinian prisoners and not allow their families visiting hours or give them proper medical care and clothes," said Abdel-Razek, a legislator and a PLO negotiator on the prisoners issue.

Asked about the allegations, Moshe Mallul, spokesman for the Israeli Prisons Authority, would relate only to the number of Palestinians who participated in the strike. He told Reuters that 1,600 had taken part.

"The most important thing is that prisoners are protesting lack of freedom. According to the PLO-Israel peace deal, they should have been freed gradually, but all that the deal reflects in prison is worse treatment," Abdel-Razek said.

Israel has freed more than 5,000 Palestinians under its interim peace accords with the PLO. But prisoner releases were frozen after a wave of suicide bombings by Moslem militants which 59 people in Israel last February and March.
Most of the Palestinian prisoners still behind bars say they belong to the mainstream Fatah faction of Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
Families of thousands of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails held a sit-in in front of the Red Cross office in Gaza City on Monday demanding improved conditions, visiting hours and their release.

"We will carry on an ongoing protest until they release our sons," said Mariam Abdallah, 65, mother of two sons serving 99 years in jail for belonging to the radical Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine.
She last visited her sons a month ago, after which Israeli authorities stopped family visits.
Huda Asana, 55, whose son belongs to Fatah and is serving 28 years in jail, said: "Our sons are sacrificed for peace. They are dying there (in jails) slowly."

In the West Bank, Birzeit University expressed "grave concern about the health and well-being of educational diploma student Mohammed Hamdan...after the Israeli High Court revoked its order of the previous day blocking the use of violence during (his interrogation)".

"This move by the High Court must be seen to further legalise the use of torture by the Israeli General Security Services...which violates basic tenants of human rights standards whch ban the use of tortuure under any circumstances," the school said in a statement on Monday.

Israel's High Court decided last week to overturn an interim court order barring the Shin Bet security service from using force to extract information from Hamdan, a suspected militant of the Islamic Jihad group.
That decision drew the attention of the United Nations Committee against Torture. One U.N. source described the court ruling as "institutionalising torture".

A 1987 Israeli commission ruled the Shin Bet could use "moderate physical pressure" in interrogations and "increased physical pressure" when an attack was imminent. Human rights groups have said the commission's report sanctioned torture.
